podcast.title: First Rock Solo on Record (1954)
podcast.body: Credited with potentially performing the first recognizable rock solo on record in 1954 on Elvis Presley's "Good Rockin' Tonight." "But it might go to Scotty Moore on Elvis Presley's Good Rockets tonight in 1954."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Guitar Style Emulation (1955)
podcast.body: After seeing Elvis perform, Sonny Curtis would borrow Buddy Holly's Fender Stratocaster to practice and play Scotty Moore's distinctive guitar licks, showcasing Moore's influence on budding rock and roll musicians. "Curtis in turn would borrow Buddy's Strat and play Scotty Moore's guitar licks."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Resignation from Elvis's Band (September 1957)
podcast.body: Scotty Moore, alongside Bill Black, resigned from Elvis's band in September 1957 due to financial grievances and frustration with Colonel Parker's control. They were placed on a salary rather than a split of earnings, suffered from a drastically cut concert schedule (only 14 shows that year), and felt unable to communicate directly with Elvis due to Parker's interference. "In September, Scotty Moore and Bill Black had written to Elvis, resigning from his band."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Career as Record Producer (Post-1958)
podcast.body: While Elvis was serving in the army, Scotty Moore transitioned into record production. He produced "Tragedy" for Thomas Wayne (Thomas Wayne Perkins), which became a pop hit, reaching number five on the charts. "Scotty became a record producer, producing the record tragedy for Thomas Wayne."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Conditions for Rejoining Elvis (1958)
podcast.body: After initially resigning, Scotty Moore was offered his job back by Elvis, who missed their stage presence. Moore's new terms included a per diem, ensuring payment regardless of performances. However, his role was diminished in the studio, where he became a regular rhythm guitarist while Hank Garland took over as the lead player on Elvis's records. "They'd be getting paid a per DM whether or not they were performing, which was something."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Work for Sam Phillips (Post-1958)
podcast.body: After his success as a producer, Scotty Moore took a job working for Sam Phillips. He continued this employment for several years, even after rejoining Elvis's studio band following Elvis's return from military service. "Scotty took a job working for Sam Phillips, and when Elvis got out of the army and Scotty rejoined him, he continued working for Phillips for a number of years."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Advice to Johnny Cash
podcast.body: After Johnny Cash saw Elvis perform, he spoke with Scotty Moore at a nightclub. Moore advised Cash to contact Sam Phillips if he wanted to get signed to Sun Records. "Moore told him to speak to Sam Phillips, and so Cash got hold of Son's phone number, and started calling, asking to speak to Phillips, who was never in."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Be-Bop-A-Lula Anecdote
podcast.body: A story circulated at the time suggesting that Scotty Moore, along with Bill Black, was annoyed with Elvis Presley for allegedly recording "Be-Bop-A-Lula" without them. This anecdote is considered unlikely to be true. "There are various stories that went round at the time, including that Scotty and Bill got annoyed as Elvis for recording it without them..."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Excluded from Film Soundtrack
podcast.body: Scotty Moore was not allowed to play on the soundtrack for Elvis Presley's first film, "Doreen O'Brothers" (later "Love Me Tender"), as the film company replaced Elvis's regular band with Hollywood session musicians. "he wasn't allowed to use Scotty Bill and DJ on the soundtrack, because the film company didn't think they could sound hillbilly enough."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Input on Chet Atkins' Production
podcast.body: Scotty Moore reported that Chet Atkins' only production advice during the "Heartbreak Hotel" session was to "just keep doing what they'd been doing." "According to Scotty Moore, his only suggestion was that they just keep doing what they'd been doing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Use of Echo and Reverb
podcast.body: Scotty Moore, a guitarist in Elvis Presley's band, was known for using echo and reverb in his sound, an element admired by East Bay Ray of the Dead Kennedys. "Another hero was Scotty Moore, who played an Elvis Presley's band, and Scotty liked to use echo and reverb in his sound, something that Ray really liked."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Musical Influences
xref.body: Growing up in a musical family, East Bay Ray was exposed to a wide range of influences, including instrumental surf rock. His heroes included Dick Dale, George Tomscow of The Fireballs, and Scotty Moore (who played in Elvis Presley's band) due to Moore's use of echo and reverb. Ray developed a distinctive guitar sound that was appealing to hardcore fans, a style heavily influenced by surf music. "He came from a musical family and was exposed to a lot of influences growing up, and that included instrumental surf rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
